appraisal_events.evidence: Aimé's letters (the doucheuse at Balbec, then the petite blanchisseuse on the Loire: « Tu me mets aux anges », « j'ai vu la morsure ») make the narrator see « la terrible nouvelle de la culpabilité d'Albertine », « une vie de mensonges et de fautes », « une vue de l'Enfer », and finally « la réalité du vice d'Albertine » — a woman who lied « comme une femme qui m'eût caché qu'elle était d'un pays ennemi et espionne », belonging « non à l'humanité commune, mais à une race étrange ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The dominant local movement is the posthumous discrediting of Albertine: she is recast, with full narratorial weight, as a habitual liar and a secretly vicious being, and pushed out of the narrator's shared humanity into an alien, guilty species.

appraisal_events.evidence: The fragmentation of Albertine restores « des moments où elle n'avait été que bonne » and « cette Albertine bonne », whose « pitié si sincère » he recalls; « Alors je ne fus plus seul ; je sentis disparaître cette cloison qui nous séparait », « la pauvre petite », « J'eus la douceur de l'entendre dire à cette Albertine-là », « je lui pardonnai » — yet framed by « on fabrique une personne, on compose un caractère ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage closes on a genuine, narrator-affirmed rehabilitation of the good Albertine, who is readmitted to the narrator's affection and forgiven; but the narrator himself immediately marks this restored figure as a construction of love and good-heartedness, so the elevation is real yet openly undercut.

status_effects.explanation: Albertine is clearly lowered in this passage: she is presented as guilty, systematically deceitful, and vicious, with her supposed innocence exposed as a lie she swore to.

At the close she is readmitted into the narrator's affective space — the dividing partition falls, he speaks to her tenderly and pardons her — partially reversing the expulsion into a foreign 'race' effected by E1.

The body of the passage leaves him tortured and powerless — burned by jealousy over a dead woman he can never confront — and the closing peace is a pardon he administers to a figure he concedes he has composed himself, so the net local movement stays mildly negative.

ambiguities: Whether the final movement (« je ne fus plus seul », « je lui pardonnai ») counts as narrator-endorsed affective renewal or as a self-consoling fabrication: the text explicitly names loving and good-heartedness as the two great sources of error and says « on fabrique une personne, on compose un caractère », so the closing turn is recorded as positive but ironized rather than as a reversal of the passage's dominant diminishment.

The evidence discrediting Albertine is hearsay relayed by Aimé (the doucheuse, then the blanchisseuse made to talk over dinner and drink), and the passage stages two counterweights — the grandmother's maxim « C'est une femme qui doit avoir la maladie du mensonge » and the imagined Albertine's charge that Aimé invented testimony to justify his fee. The diminishment is still read as endorsed because the narrating voice ultimately treats « la réalité du vice d'Albertine » as established fact.
